title: Secret agent bot: accessibility matters for the agents even if you can’t see them
text:
Secret agent bot: accessibility matters for the agents even if you can’t see them

The semantic structure screen readers have used for decades now also decide whether ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity can read your page at all.

In 2016 I had a series of calls with the federal government’s top accessibility expert as the leader of a design team, and I learned more in those conversations than in years of reading specifications. I had already been building accessible web applications since 2006, chasing Level AAA when most teams would not commit to AA. I learned so much, and it’s always been top of mind.

The lede even back then: accessibility matters, and we should pay attention to it.

For a long time that work served a small, often-overlooked audience you defended on principle alone.

That argument just changed just got larger.

Your website has a new kind of visitor, and it does not look at your page the way you do. It reads a stripped-down model of the page called the accessibility tree — the same structure browsers have built for screen readers for two decades. It doesn’t know what a color is; it looks for well-labeled structure.

If you don’t have it, it can’t find you. And most sites don’t have it.

The numbers: In early June 2026, Cloudflare reported that automated traffic had passed human traffic on the web for the first time, roughly 57 percent of page requests against 43 percent.

A fast-growing share of web traffic is agents acting for people.

The audience that reads through structure of your pages to understand context is no longer a rounding error, it is most of your traffic. Welcome to inclusive design. The questions narrow: which agents read what, when accessibility becomes load-bearing, and the small set of categories worth fixing first.

I’ll be covering all of the major agents on how they read a page in a later series of articles because it’s fascinating, but this is a good place to start.

How the Major Vendors Read a Page

There are three ways an agent can take in a page: it can look at a screenshot with a vision model, read the raw HTML of the document, or read the accessibility tree the browser builds from that HTML.

Each has a cost.

A screenshot is expensive in tokens and easy to misread when layouts are dense. Raw HTML is noisy, thousands of tokens of wrappers and scripts around the few elements that matter, frankly because of poor engineering practices and human slop code.

The accessibility tree is the cheap, clean option: a short list of the interactive elements, their roles, their names, and their states. Google’s own guidance for developers is that capable agents combine all three, leaning on the structured channels and using the picture to confirm layout. That’s pricey, and also means 3 different results.

The vendors split on where they start

  • Anthropic’s Computer Use is vision-first: Claude looks at screenshots and counts pixels to place the cursor, which is flexible but fragile when the screen shifts. Its browser extension, Claude in Chrome, leans the other way — its read_page tool takes the accessibility tree first, with a get_page_text tool for article-style pages and screenshots as the fallback.
  • Microsoft went the other way, at least for developers. Its Playwright MCP, the official server for letting a model drive a browser, works from structured accessibility snapshots and skips vision entirely, on the stated premise that the structured view beats a screenshot. Its consumer surface is the opposite: in Copilot Mode in Edge, Copilot Actions read and act inside your signed-in session, leaning on what is on screen.
  • Google’s Gemini agents sit in the hybrid middle. It blends the structured channels with a visual pass to confirm what the layout is doing rather than committing to one or the other. For users that shows up as Gemini in Chrome and its Auto Browse mode, with Project Mariner as the research agent behind it.
  • The most telling case is OpenAI. Its Computer-Using Agent, which drives both Operator and the Atlas browser, started from screenshots. OpenAI’s own publisher guidance now tells site owners that Atlas uses ARIA tags, the same labels and roles that support screen readers, to interpret page structure, and points them to standard accessibility practices. Even the company whose agent leads with pixels is telling you to fix your accessibility tree.

When Accessibility Becomes Foundational

Accessibility does not matter equally on every page, and it is worth being precise about where it does.

For a page that is mostly prose, an agent can usually cope; the words are the content, and even a messy structure leaves them readable. The stakes rise the moment the agent has to act — to find the right button, fill the correct field, choose among options, and move through a flow without losing its place.

Transactional, multi-step, and dynamic interfaces are where a broken structure stops being an inconvenience and starts being a brick wall.

If a keyboard user cannot finish the task, the agent usually cannot either.

The evidence is getting concrete. In the A11y-CUA study presented at CHI 2026, researchers at UC Berkeley and the University of Michigan ran Claude Sonnet 4.5 through 60 everyday web and desktop tasks under different conditions.

  • With normal access the agent finished about 78 percent of them.
  • Constrained to keyboard-only navigation — the path an accessibility-tree agent depends on — success fell to 42 percent, and the work took roughly twice as long.
  • Under a magnified viewport it dropped to 28 percent.

The same structural gaps that strand a screen-reader user strand the agent. If a keyboard user cannot finish the task, the agent usually cannot either. Accessible structure is not a separate track from agent-readiness; it is the track.

Legibility Is Not Endorsement

Building a page an agent can read is not the same as endorsing every agent that reads it. Anil Dash has argued that some of these products are openly hostile to the open web, substituting synthesized summaries for the pages and links underneath.

Legibility and approval are different things.

He is right that legibility and approval are different things. You can make your page structurally honest and still decide a given browser is a bad deal for the web, and hold the two judgments apart. The discipline stands on its own terms: it serves the people using assistive technology no matter what you make of any agent.

The Nielsen Norman Group makes the parallel case from the design side, treating agents as a class of user you now serve whether you meant to or not — which is a reason to build for them, not a verdict on them.

There is a sharper version of the cost, and it cuts against the grain of this whole piece. A page that is accessible and semantically correct is the easiest kind of page for an AI assistant to read, summarize, and answer from — which makes it the easiest kind to lift without sending anyone your way.

Do the structural work well and the assistant may cite you, paraphrase you, and keep the user inside its own answer.

It’s literally reverse SEO — honor the standards and pay the cost. Welcome to the world of AI.

The same legibility that wins the agent can cost you the click, and the ranking that used to come with it. That is a real tradeoff, not a reason to ship a broken page, but go in with your eyes open.

Where To Start

Category One: Semantic Structure and Landmarks

This is the foundation, and the cheapest win. Native HTML elements announce themselves in the accessibility tree without any extra work. A <button> is a button the agent can find and trust.

A <div> wired up with a click handler is an unnamed, role-less box the agent has to guess about, and it guesses wrong often enough to matter. The web.dev guidance is unglamorous on purpose: use the element that means what you intend, and most of the structure takes care of itself.

Two things sit on top of that foundation. Headings are the outline an agent reads to understand what a page contains and how its parts relate; a logical order, h1 to h2 to h3 without skipped levels, gives the agent a map instead of a pile.

Landmarks — navigation, main, header, footer — tell it which region it is standing in.

None of this is new advice. It is the same structure the field has taught for years, now with a second reader who takes it literally.

Category Two: Names, Roles, and States

Every control an agent might use needs a name in the tree, a role that says what it is, and — when it changes — a state that says what it is doing now. This is where most real pages fail. Icon-only buttons with no label, links that all read “read more,” custom dropdown menusand modals built from generic markup: each one lands in the accessibility tree as a blank or a question mark.

The agent can see that something is there and cannot tell what it does.

ARIA exists to fill the gaps native HTML cannot express — to give a custom widget the role and state it would otherwise lack. But it comes with a sharp rule the vendors tend to skip past.

The First Rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA: if a native element already carries the meaning, use it, because a wrong or empty ARIA attribute is worse than none.

It does not leave the tree blank; it fills the tree with confident, incorrect information, and the agent has no way to know it is being misled. OpenAI’s guidance tells publishers to reach for ARIA. Accessibility practitioners have pushed back that the durable fix is correct markup, not bolt-on attributes — and the data is on their side.

Here is the part that should bother you. In 2026, web accessibility got worse for the first time in six years. WebAIM’s annual scan of the top million home pages found detectable WCAG failures on 95.9 percent of them, up from 94.8 percent, with the average page carrying about 56 errors across 1,437 elements — a 22.5 percent jump in page complexity in a single year. ARIA usage climbed 27 percent, and the pages reaching hardest for it carried the most errors.

WebAIM names a likely culprit: AI-assisted coding. The same wave of agents now reading your page is helping generate the broken structure that makes it unreadable.

We’ll talk about that harness needed in a later article.

Category Three: Text Alternatives and Labels

This category is about the content that is real on the page but invisible in the structure unless you make it explicit. Images are the obvious case: without alternative text, an agent cannot tell a product photo from a logo from a chart, and a linked image with no alt text becomes a link to nowhere. WebAIM still finds missing alternative text among the most common failures on the web, year after year.

An agent cannot fill a field it cannot name.

Form fields are the same problem in a different place. An agent cannot fill a field it cannot name, so a label tied to its input is the difference between a completed checkout and an abandoned one.

The fix is dull and well understood: real alternative text on meaningful images, an empty alt on decorative ones, and a programmatic label on every input.

Category Four: Feedback and Stable Layout

The last category is about what happens after the agent acts. State has to be announced, not just shown. If a confirmation appears only as a visual change, the agent acts as if nothing happened.

If a confirmation appears only as a visual change, the agent acts as if nothing happened.

A result, an error, or a status update that never reaches the tree leaves the agent guessing; live regions and managed focus are how you tell it the page moved.

And layout has to hold still.

Agents that fall back to a screenshot lose their footing when the same control sits in a different place on every page, so consistency stops being a matter of polish and becomes a matter of whether the agent can find the thing at all.

The Work Is Already Specified and Has Been For Years

Here is the reassuring part, rare in a piece about new technology. You are not being asked to optimize for some proprietary new format. The thing agents need from your page is the thing the accessibility community has asked for all along: semantic markup, named controls, real text alternatives, honest state, stable layout.

That work used to pay once, for the people using assistive technology. Now it pays twice, because the same structure is what the machines read.

So treat it as triage, not a rebuild. Do not try to agent-proof every page. Find the flows where an agent has to act — the checkout, the booking, the account change — and make those legible first.

Open your browser’s developer tools, look at the accessibility tree for that flow, and ask whether you could finish the task from the tree alone. Then walk it with the keyboard only. Where you hit a wall, so does the agent.

The audience that reads through structure was easy to ignore when it was small. It is not small anymore. The web you can see is increasingly the smaller half of the room, and the other half is reading the tree you built — or the one you didn’t.

Here’s What to Consider

Before you change anything, weigh these:

  • Whether an agent would act on the page, not just read it. Static prose is low-stakes; the checkout, the booking, and the account change are where structure turns load-bearing.
  • Whether you could finish the key flow from the accessibility tree alone. Open your developer tools, look, and then walk the same flow with the keyboard only. Where you stall, the agent stalls.
  • Whether every control has a name, a role, and a state. Icon-only buttons and links that all read “read more” are the blanks that strand an agent.
  • Whether you are reaching for ARIA to patch markup that should be native. A wrong or empty attribute is worse than none, because it fills the tree with confident, incorrect information.
  • Whether images, fields, and feedback are spelled out. Alt text, tied labels, and announced state are what keep them from being invisible in the structure.
  • Whether the layout holds still across similar pages. An agent that falls back to a screenshot loses its place when the same control moves.
  • Whether legibility means endorsement. It does not — you can build an honest page and still judge a given agent a bad deal for the web.

Turns Out, All We Need This Season Is A Sweater In This It Color

If you thought the color of the season was burgundy or forest green or burnt orange, think again. This fall, a bolder hue is hitting the runways, stores, streets, and now our closets: deep purple. In the past month, shades of vibrant violet, witchy plum, and striking indigo have found their way onto the Spring/Summer 2027 runways and many street style icons.

First, New York Fashion Week spotlighted bold purple across more than 20 designer collections, including Sergio Hudson, Diane von Furstenberg, and Christian Cowan, notably styled with poppy red and vivid teal. Tory Burch sent a purple sweater down the runway with an on-trend red skirt. Then, we quickly noticed the showgoers donning the color too (I even incorporated purple into my final-day ‘fit because of it). And it didn’t stop there. During Milan and Paris fashion weeks, the likes of Miu Miu, Prada, Balmain, Bottega Veneta, Valentino, and Issey Miyake had pops of purple in their new collections.

And now, purple has seeped all over our feeds, thanks to trend forecasters, influencers and our favorite celebrities, including Zoë Kravitz wearing it. But we’ve particularly noticed an influx in purple sweaters as the go-to way to wear the color. J.Crew even recently released its viral Rollneck sweater in a vibrant purple and it immediately sold out. (But you can still pre-order the style in a muted eggplant shade.)

So, whether it’s a crewneck worn with a collared button-down underneath, a short-sleeve turtleneck paired with a pencil skirt, or a chunky cardigan unbuttoned over a red tank top, there are seemingly no rules. It can be as cheerful or as spooky as you’d like. And whichever way it’s styled, a purple sweater has proved itself to be a piece that’s simultaneously a statement and a versatile staple that you need in your closet.

To help you get the look, we’ve searched for the best options on the market, from a $70 lightweight Zara turtleneck to a $550 wool Staud cardigan, all purple-lover-approved.

title: The Secret To Making $65 Basics Look Expensive
text:
The Secret To Making $65 Basics Look Expensive

There’s a particular kind of satisfaction in telling someone that this was only $65, especially after they’ve complimented your outfit. Because looking expensive has surprisingly little to do with how much you spend. More often, it comes down to knowing what to pair together.

That’s the thinking behind the high-low formula: start with the uncomplicated pieces that earn their keep in your closet (you know your white T-shirts, your go-to sweatpants, and your cozy hoodies), then introduce something with a little more pizzazz into the look. Maybe it’s a sharply tailored blazer, a great leather bag, an unexpected mini skirt, or playful lace-up flats. Mixing and matching these key pieces is every fashion girl’s secret to looking like a style star.

Nike makes an especially good starting point for this approach. Its sporty staples already have the clean lines and relaxed proportions that are crucial to the backbones of a well-curated collection of basics. So instead of saving your sweats for the couch or your crewneck for errands, consider them the first layer of a much better outfit. Below, five formulas for making everyday essentials look considerably more expensive than they are.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Simple Tee + The Boxy Blazer + The Sweatpants

The quickest way to make sweatpants feel effortlessly cool, never slouchy is by giving them something structured to play against. A boxy blazer instantly sharpens the softness of a relaxed pant, while a fitted white tee gives the layers underneath simple vigor. From there, resist the urge to make everything else casual. A sleek clutch, sculptural earrings, dark sunglasses, and pointed-toe mules create the kind of contrast that will instantly turn you into a fashion girlie.

The Crewneck + Slip Skirt + Leather Bag

A sweatshirt and satin skirt shouldn’t necessarily work together, which is precisely why the do. The relaxed, slightly sporty attitude of an oversized crewneck takes some of the preciousness out of a silky midi, while the skirt gives an everyday top a completely different context. Add a polished leather shoulder bag and slim sunglasses to keep things sophisticated, then ground the look with a sneaker rather than a heel. The result lands somewhere between dressed up and completely unbothered (arguably the best place for an outfit to be).

The Simple Tank + Wide-Leg Trouser + Statement Belt

A great tank top doesn’t need much help, but it does benefit from a strong silhouette around it. Pairing a close-fitting tank with exaggerated wide-leg trousers creates instant proportion and makes a relatively simple combination look far more directional. A statement belt gives the eye somewhere to land and helps define the waist against all that volume. Finish with a compact bag, minimalist sunglasses, and a low heel. Nothing here is particularly complicated.

The Sweatpants + The Trench + The Pretty Flats

Consider this your argument for wearing sweats somewhere other than the airport. A trench coat brings instant polish to a matching hoodie-and-pant combination, but the real trick is what happens below the ankle. Instead of defaulting to sneakers, add delicate flats (I, personally, can’t resist a lace-up ballerina). That tension between sporty and pretty makes the entire ensemble interesting. A shoulder bag and barely-there sunglasses finish things off without competing with the unexpected color underneath.

The Quarter Zip + The Mini Skirt + The Loafers

The quarter-zip has officially escaped the gym bag. Paired with a clean A-line mini, its athletic associations start to feel almost preppy, particularly when loafers enter the equation. Keeping the palette tonal makes the inexpensive pieces read as one cohesive look rather than a collection of separates. Then add the details that make minimal outfits matter: a substantial leather tote, scrunched socks, and classic frames. Together, it’s proof that basics don’t have to be boring at all. Sometimes all they need is better company.

title: Johanna Toruño Wants Latinas To Take Up More Space
text:
Johanna Toruño Wants Latinas To Take Up More Space

Growing up, I tried my very best to take up as little space as possible wherever I was. I didn’t want to be seen, so I minimized every part of myself. I covered the curves I was inheriting from my Puerto Rican mother under oversized sweatshirts during sweltering Orlando summers, and, not long after, spent years shrinking myself in ways that took a serious toll on my body and my life. I spoke softly. I held in coughs until they became that little scratchy tickle at the back of my throat, and I attempted to muffle my loud, disruptive laugh behind my hand, practically suffocating myself so I wouldn’t be heard.

As Latinas, we’ve been taught, in both subtle and explicit ways, that being too visible, too loud, too opinionated, too ambitious, just too much can come with consequences. We are taught there is safety in being agreeable and virtue in being selfless. And so we disappear, both literally and figuratively, both physically and emotionally. 

And right now, as our community is being targeted by immigration crackdowns, threats to our rights, and political rhetoric increasingly telling us that we don’t belong, that pressure to disappear can feel even more intense. Research shows that when you’re living with immigration anxiety, or the fear of being stopped, detained, watched, or profiled, it can change how you move through the world, where you go, how you show up, and even how comfortable you feel taking up space.

But what parts of ourselves do we lose when we’re constantly trying to be less and what could our communities gain if more of us felt free to take up space?

In today’s episode of Sin Vergüenza by Somos, we’re getting into all the messages and expectations that teach us to make ourselves smaller and learning how to resist them and, instead, take up more space, for ourselves and for each other. To do that, we’re speaking with Johanna Toruño, the queer Salvadoran-born, Virginia-raised, and LA-based artist behind The Unapologetic Street Series, a project she started in 2016 that uses public spaces across the country as a canvas for affirmations celebrating Latinas, immigrants, queer and trans people, and other marginalized communities. 

In this episode, we get into the expectation put on Latinas to not take up space, how we can begin to unlearn it, making ourselves visible even when it’s scary, and inspiring other Latinas to do the same.

title: A Sexologist On Why Reading Smut Is Good For You (And Where To Start)
text:
A Sexologist On Why Reading Smut Is Good For You (And Where To Start)

Sex education taught me what an erection was, but smut taught me about desire. Most of us got the mechanics, the risks and a condom on a banana. What we didn’t get was anything about wanting, so many of us went looking for that in books and fanfics. Smut is fiction where sex is part of the story, but I think it can do something more interesting than simply give you something sexy to read. It can give you somewhere to figure yourself out.

You don’t need me to tell you smut is having a moment. In the US, print romance sales jumped 24% in a year, with 51 million books sold in a year. Romantasy (romance plus fantasy, usually plus dragons or fae) was the fastest-growing category in the whole print market in 2024. To me, those numbers mean millions of people choosing to spend time in stories about wanting, being wanted, and exploring something new. And that makes my sexologist heart sing.

Fantasy and desire matter

A lot of the pleasure in a smutty book comes from making you wait, in the build-up between the two main characters, the almost-touch, knowing what’s coming and having to wait for it; a good smutty book can spend 300 pages there. And if you’ve ever wondered why one scene works for you while another leaves you completely cold, that’s part of the answer: arousal has a context. It might be the way someone looks at you, a particular voice, the tension of a power dynamic, or the feeling of being wanted. Smut gives you a safer space to notice that, to play with that feeling of, oh… that’s doing something to me.

That’s one reason reading is a much lower-stakes place than real life to explore desire. Nobody’s watching, you don’t have to do anything for anybody else, you don’t have to explain yourself, and you can close the book whenever you like. That’s important because it’s a place to learn that fantasies aren’t contractual — you can be turned on by the idea of something without wanting it in real life. Researcher Justin Lehmiller surveyed more than 4,000 people about their fantasies and found that nearly everyone has them (97%), and found an enormous range in what people imagined wanting. This research is a useful reminder that fantasies play a different role for all of us. It might be a new idea, something to try, or it might be something that plays out beautifully in your head but something you’d never want to do in person. And that’s totally fine.

Don’t skip fanfic

Fanfiction often gets left out of these conversations, and it shouldn’t. So many of us who love smut grew up in the Tumblr era of fanfiction (cough, One Direction fanfic, cough). Fanfic has always been particularly good at letting people take characters they already care about and put them into the stories they wanted to see. Archive of Our Own (AO3) hosts more than 18 million works; it’s run by volunteers, and it’s free.

It also does something the rest of erotic media could learn from. Every story is tagged — who’s in it, what happens, how explicit it gets, what you might want a warning for. You know what you’re opting into before you read a word, and you can filter out anything you never want to see (consent icons). I think it’s one of the best informed-choice systems going.

Fanfic also gives people a place to read desire that looks like theirs. Queer, disabled, and neurodivergent readers have been writing themselves into these kinds of stories on there for years, because mainstream romance and erotic media didn’t give them enough places to see themselves in this context.

If you’ve never read smut before, here are five tips to get started

Start with a trope: enemies to lovers, only one bed, fake dating — if a set-up already does something for you, follow it.

Go short: A novella or a 5,000-word fic is a much smaller ask than a 600-page romantasy.

Listen instead: Audiobooks and audio erotica count, and they’re a good option if reading doesn’t work for you.

Pick your own spice level: Reviews and tags will usually tell you how explicit something gets before you start.

Stop if it’s not working: you don’t owe a book a finish (not a bad rule for sex either).

Start with these smutty books and fanfics

Fourth Wing and Iron Flame by Rebecca Yarros.
I am a lover of the Empyrean series. Dragons, a war college, and Shadow Daddy, I won’t be expanding further.

The Love Hypothesis by Ali Hazelwood
Loved this one. Fake dating in a science lab, and it started life as fanfic, which tells you where a lot of the good stuff comes from.

A Game of Hearts and Heists by Ruby Roe
A Sapphic fantasy with a disgraced assassin, her rival poisoner, a heist and only one bed.

if i bleed you’ll be the last to know by spaceprincessem (AO3)
For the teenwolf fans, Derek & Stiles.

if i don’t make it back from where i’ve gone, just know i loved you all along by whiry (AO3)
For The Witcher fans, Jaskier & Geralt.

Leather & Lace on Dipsea.
For when you’d rather listen — “Sebastian & Benj give Jackie exactly what she wants, and then some…” need I say more?

Sometimes the thing you learn from smut is that you really, really like a particular fictional man being told what to do. Sometimes you learn something a little more personal: what makes you curious, what makes you want to keep reading, and what you’d happily leave on the page. Either way, I think that’s a pretty good reason to keep a little smut on your bookshelf.

title: Taylor Polidore Williams On Finding Her Voice at an HBCU
text:
Taylor Polidore Williams On Finding Her Voice at an HBCU

There’s a moment that comes for every woman when she looks around and realizes that she is, somehow, some way, the adult in the room. Hosts Sandy Pierre and Kathleen Newman-Bremang chat with actress and advocate Taylor Polidore Williams about what it takes to become the person you needed when you were young.  

You may recognize Polidore Williams from the hit shows Beauty in Black and Reasonable Doubt, but what you may not know is that she is a proud alumna of Clark Atlanta University. “It’s such a huge part of what has helped me find my voice, my confidence,” she says of her time at CAU. “The experience of going to an HBCU is like no other, just because I think it’s one of the only places in the world literally where your race isn’t a factor.” Though she started acting at a young age, Williams found that both the city of Atlanta and CAU fostered her drive; she was in a place where her determination was celebrated and nurtured. It helped shape her into the woman and artist she is today. “When you know yourself, and you’ve had the experience to come into your own and try things out and fail, and having professors be like, ‘you can do better than that.’ That type of refinement lets you come into the world with ‘I might face all these different things, but I know in this community I’m seen.’”  

“Some things you only learn through experience; I don’t regret the ambition I had back then.” Williams goes on to say, “Right now the goal is specificity in my journey.” Right now, that journey includes supporting the next generation through Shelter Rock Foundation, which supports and nurtures youth in the foster system. The foundation also recently launched a housing scholarship for three media arts students at CAU, because let’s be real: the rent is too damn high and it’s hard to be creative when you’re worrying about bills.  

As Williams, Pierre, and Newman-Bremang share stories of fighting for internships, working their way up in the world, and realizing that they’re no longer the babygirl, they revel in the ways that others have helped them along the way. Alongside the many mentors and family members who have given her advice, Williams reflects on Clark Atlanta University, which “has carried me through a lot of things in life, because even if you don’t necessarily see a way, there’s always a way.”
